identityReview: Gillian Doreen Triggs, born in London on 30 October 1945, Australian international-law scholar and former AHRC president (30 July 2012–2017). Former Sydney dean/Challis professor, former BIICL director and former UN Assistant Secretary-General serving as UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection from September 2019 to December 2023 according to the specific chronology. Current Australia for UNHCR Patron, not a current UNHCR executive, high commissioner, government minister or elected parliamentarian. The undergraduate law degree is confirmed but its 1967/1968 year is unresolved; PhD 1982 is supported by NLA, AHRC and Melbourne.
lifeStatusEvidence: AAP’s 18 September 2026 report explicitly quotes comments she made to the agency on earlier child detention in the context of newly announced migration measures. This is an actual reported interview, not a future event announcement or an inference from a reused portrait.

sourceReview.accessMethod: Read the relevant NLA and AHRC biographies, Melbourne interview introduction, World Bank speaker biography, inquiry chronology and factsheet sections, ABC controversy report, Triggs honours entry in the Governor-General PDF, Sydney honours announcement, Australia for UNHCR Patron entry, Melbourne 2026 fellowship announcement and AAP report. Additional access results and indexed-only evidence are separately recorded. No original portrait pixels or audiovisual recordings were reviewed.
corrections: Read the National Library biography sections on early life, education and career. It gives birth in Muswell Hill, London, on 30 October 1945, migration with her family in 1958, a 1972 Southern Methodist University LLM and a 1982 Melbourne doctorate on territorial sovereignty. Its first law-degree year is 1968, whereas Melbourne’s alumni interview gives 1967; omit the disputed undergraduate year rather than silently choosing one. It dates the public-international-law professorship to 1996–2005, BIICL leadership to 2005–2007, Sydney deanship to 2007–2012 and commencement of the five-year AHRC presidency to 30 July 2012. It explicitly states that her UNHCR term ended in December 2023. Embedded oral-history recordings were not listened to or treated as reviewed transcripts.

Read the AHRC archived former-president biography. The 2012–2017 presidency and prior academic leadership are historical, not current appointments. Its Melbourne LLB year is 1968 and PhD year 1982; the conflicting undergraduate year is left unspecified. The temporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner assignment from August 2016 to February 2017 is not a permanent second presidency or an elected office. Historic advisory and board roles in this archived biography are not automatically current as of November 2026.

Read the introduction and career summary of the Melbourne Law School alumni interview. It labels the LLB 1967 and PhD 1982, and confirms the 1996–2005 professorship. The undergraduate-year discrepancy with AHRC and NLA is explicitly preserved; the degree itself is established. The Geneva interview context and then-current UN title are historical. The full interview and any associated audiovisual material were not exhaustively reviewed.

Read the World Bank Live speaker biography. It explicitly dates the start of her UNHCR appointment to September 2019 and describes protection responsibilities for refugees, asylum-seekers, internally displaced people and stateless people. Its present-tense UN title is stale and is not used as current-office evidence. Assistant Secretary-General is her UN rank and Assistant High Commissioner for Protection her UNHCR office; neither is Secretary-General, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights nor UN High Commissioner for Refugees. Its mention of the Asian Development Bank Administrative Tribunal concerns a tribunal, not presidency of the bank. British/Australian dual nationality is mentioned, while the profile’s country field identifies her Australian public career without asserting exclusive citizenship.

Read the AHRC inquiry page’s scope, hearings and report chronology. Launch was 3 February 2014, delivery to the attorney-general 11 November 2014, and tabling in federal parliament 11 February 2015. Page-category labels such as January 2014 and related-document dates do not replace these explicit event dates. The inquiry concerned children in closed immigration detention; community detention was outside its scope. Its five public hearings and submissions belong to this historical inquiry, not a new 2026 investigation. Linked full reports and all witness transcripts were not read.

Read relevant findings, methods and chronology in the July 2015 factsheet. It combines detention-centre visits, interviews with children and parents, medical consultants, submissions and sworn hearings. Counts of interviews are not all children, and 2014/2015 detention populations are not current counts. Its findings about physical and mental harm and treaty obligations are the commission’s findings, not a new court judgment or proof that every later government measure is unlawful. The report’s delivery and tabling dates match the inquiry overview. The full inquiry and underlying medical case records were not independently audited.

Read ABC’s 25 February 2015 account of the political controversy. Abbott and Brandis challenged the commission president’s impartiality and said they had lost confidence; Turnbull urged attention to children and acknowledged her academic standing. Claims and denials concerning a possible alternative role and resignation were contested at the time; no bribery, criminal conviction or proven dismissal is inferred. The public dossier records the disagreement over evidence and independence, without presenting a partisan accusation as fact. ABC also gives the LLB year as 1967, reinforcing the need not to force a single disputed undergraduate year.

Read the Gillian Doreen Triggs entry and citation in the Governor-General’s 2025 honours media notes. It lists Companion in the General Division and recognises work across humanitarian/human-rights law, international relations, social justice and legal education/research. The PDF’s February URL or revision date is not the 26 January honours announcement, independently confirmed by Sydney. Its biographical list gives UN roles as 2019–2024, whereas NLA explicitly identifies completion in December 2023 and the indexed UNHCR closing statement says retirement at the end of 2023; use the more specific endpoint and preserve this discrepancy. Other recipients’ entries were not reviewed or attributed to Triggs.

Read the University of Sydney’s 26 January 2025 honours announcement and the Triggs entry. It confirms the AC appointment, the announcement date, former dean/Challis chair roles and former AHRC/UNHCR roles. It does not claim she became a new UN office-holder in 2025 or received an academic degree with the honour. Companion is an Order of Australia grade, not a British damehood or an honorary doctorate. The citation is paraphrased; awards and biographies of other recipients are not attributed to her.

Read the Australia for UNHCR page’s Triggs section. Although the URL refers to ambassadors, her explicit heading is Patron and the text dates this role to 2024. It is a role in the Australian refugee-support organisation, not a renewed UN executive appointment, a UN goodwill-ambassador designation or diplomatic ambassadorship. The current listing supports the patron role; older descriptions of her as an ambassador do not override the specific current label. Its past-award and memoir mentions are not used to invent new publication or award dates.

Read the Melbourne announcement listing eight academics elected in the Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia’s 2026 intake, including Triggs. Use the year only because a precise announcement or election day was not established. This is fellowship of the social-sciences academy, not the Australian Academy of Science, a new doctorate or proof of attendance at a future ceremony. The accomplishments of the other seven people are not attributed to her.

Read the 18 September 2026 AAP report by Will Nicholas and Noah Secomb on The Queenslander, including its actual interview quotations and government response. Triggs personally commented on past child-detention harm, establishing recent activity; the accompanying photo alone is not the evidence. Her number of detained children refers to the earlier inquiry, not 2026. The announced visa-overstayer plan, proposed beds and compliance staff are not established completed implementation, and comments by the Greens senator are not attributed to Triggs. The 2023 High Court ruling is background whose application to the new plan was described as uncertain; no independent legal conclusion about the proposal is asserted.

additionalConsulted.access: Search result identifies the 8 August 2019 appointment announcement, but open returned only a three-line shell without substantive body. Do not claim the announcement was fully read or use announcement date as the September start date.
Returned 429 on two attempts. The independently readable World Bank biography supports September 2019 commencement; no claim to have read the UNHCR release body.

Direct open returned 429. A later search-index excerpt of Grandi’s 15 December 2023 statement explicitly thanks Triggs and says she will retire at year end; this is indexed corroboration, not a full direct-page read. NLA explicitly records completed service in December 2023.

Read the short Gazette notice dated 26 January 2025 and published under a 28 January path. It announces award categories and links to recipient lists; it does not itself name Triggs, so Sydney and the Governor-General entry supply person-specific confirmation.

Read relevant retrospective sections mentioning her keynote earlier that month. Quoted comments were described as made ahead of the event, not a verified transcript of delivery. The church committee’s advocacy and proposed legislation are not independent court findings or proof the bill became law. The article’s publication date is not a precise date of her personal appearance.

Read the 18 July 2026 programme metadata and description. No audio was listened to; no quotation or full transcript is claimed. Its additional board-role wording was not separately verified for the November cutoff and is not promoted into a current-office claim.
File page inaccessible via web open; old local licence metadata remains unrefreshed. Category search snippets are not substitutes for full provenance or pixels.
Original photographer/source-page link was inaccessible. Licence and attribution chain still require a readable source and actual image inspection.

sourceReview.limits: AI editorial and translation review, not certified native-language human review. No complete inquiry-report audit, private medical records, full witness transcripts, original degree certificate, complete UN personnel file, current migration-law analysis, audio/video recordings or portrait pixels were reviewed. Preserve the undergraduate-year and UN end-year discrepancies in the audit record; use verified education without a disputed undergraduate year and the specific December 2023 endpoint. Refresh current affiliations and activity before publication.

Search-index category listings confirm the filename and dimensions but cannot verify the current full file page or original attribution. Their 2.12 MB figure and the old cached-image index’s 351984 bytes may describe different representations; without bytes do not infer a changed original. The referenced cache is absent. The original request returned curl 22, HTTP 403 and reported HTTP 000 on 18 November. Capture date versus upload/version timestamp, licence chain, photographer credit, depicted identity, colour, crop and resolution remain to be checked.

translationReview.scope: All 32 display fields in seven foreign languages reviewed against Chinese and the English intermediary. Preserve birth/migration dates; verified degrees without choosing the disputed undergraduate year; international public-law professorship and academic roles; inquiry launch, attorney-general delivery and parliamentary tabling as separate events; political criticism as attributed disagreement; AHRC presidency versus elected/ministerial office; Assistant Secretary-General rank versus UNHCR protection office; September 2019 start and December 2023 end; nonprofit Patron versus UN ambassador/executive; 2025 AC honour versus academic degree; 2026 social-sciences fellowship; historical child-detention counts versus current statistics.
